questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Prior to studying abroad, I had always been interested in Japanese culture and had visited the country before. I saw it as great opportunity to broaden my worldview, explore an interesting culture and also gain new academic knowledge. Additionally, it will enhance career opportunities.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a wonderful time overall. I gained a lot of new friendships, broadened my understanding of the world and traveled a lot around Japan. If you're interested in traveling to other Asian countries, that's also possible. The only major negative thing affecting my rating would be the amount of subjects relevant to my major, but I then had the opportunity to try other interesting courses.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: They provided a student handbook with a lot of information and had an office one could go for help, however I was still confused about some aspects.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a ceremony and Zoom meeting, however I was confused about some aspects of the course registrations because it was so different. They did not disclose how many courses I needed, and neither could KU, which created a lot of trouble getting my courses accepted for credits. So for almost 4 months I did not know whether my courses would count for credits or not.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it through my host institution. I had to do a lottery, stating my housing priorities as well as habits (smoking/drinking), noise sensitivity, mobility and whether I take any medicine. Lotteries are very widespread in Japan, so one has to get used to that. It dragged out the housing situation a lot, which I did not appreciate.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I was lucky to receive a room at WID Waseda, which is <5 min away from campus on foot. It provided meals (if one wishes), high security and modern facilities, so living off campus was very hassle-free.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Maybe my memory is fuzzy, but it would have been nice to have a complete map with the distance to campus.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It's an online lottery system which is very confusing. You don't know whether you will get the courses you applied for or not, so the right strategy is to apply to as many as possible so you can drop courses after gaining a spot (there are several rounds). I did not know this strategy, which resulted in not getting some courses I really wanted.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not a lot. I had to ask fellow students for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got most of what I wanted (although it was very limited for my major), but I did not receive one specific course I really wanted, sadly.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Apply for as many courses as possible and then drop the ones you don't need/want after.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: My graduate school is an English program, so 9/10 were international students. This means a lot of different English levels, which can affect the quality of discussions. I would say the overall course level is a bit lower, and the grading is a lot easier than in Denmark.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Very different. At KU, I'm used to 1 presentations per course per semester, but at Waseda I had a lot more, but it depends on the courses, of course. I'm also used to not having a lot of assignments, but since you have more courses at Waseda, the workload is spread out and you have more homework per week. I had 17 assignments in total, 8 presentations and 4 final term papers.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Language and Mind, Cultural Critical Theories 2, International Cooperation and Peacebuilding and Race and Ethnicity.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: International Cooperation and Peacebuilding was nice because you gained a wider perspective of the world.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The high cost of housing is mainly due to the entrance fees, management fees, cleaning fees etc. For the boarding itself, it was only around 5300 kr. a month. I also had to pay for a VPN in order to bypass some censorship from the Japanese government.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Fruit and vegetables are expensive. Eating out is affordable (25-75 kr). Domestic traveling can be very expensive, but it depends on the transportation chosen. Getting to Japan can be very expensive due to the distance. Phone plan is expensive and data is very slow in urban places.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were opportunities but not a lot of for English-speaking students. The orientation at the beginning of the semester gives you an overview of some of the circles/clubs.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Plenty of sports circles.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sports clubs, the language and culture exchange buddy program in order to gain more friendships since it can be a little difficult with Japanese people (just like it is in Denmark!)

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to an izakaya with friends, explore cafés and museums. See some of the 80.000 shrines and travel around the country, even for day trips outside Tokyo. Each city is known for something else.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I was pretty familiar with Japanese culture but I still had to get used to the way of communicating (despite reading about it) and the usage of cash, slow bureaucracy and print-based systems. The social rules are very strong and you are expected to follow them, or else there will be consequences.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Put yourself out there. Befriend someone they know to have a common link or join a club you can bond through. Join a buddy program.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Indirect communication, strict rules about what is considered rude (don't eat/drink while walking, certain way of eating, greetings, etc.). Not helping strangers in need.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Order and punctuality.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: (1) Prioritize your time right or you will run out of time to explore Japan. (2) Make local friends, they will enhance your experience of the country a lot. The possible friendships are truly wonderful. (3) Learn at least some basic Japanese or you will struggle.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Get a credit or debit card capable of using Yen. I used WISE to convert DKK to Yen. It will save you a lot of transaction fees.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: New relationships and wonderful memories. You also become a lot more open-minded and independent.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not seeing loved-ones at home and doing everything by yourself in a different language.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Remember that you represent a country and am a guest. Respect the local culture.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
